name: Esther
author: The writer of Esther is not named. Jewish tradition credits the book to the 'Men of the Great Assembly,' a council of Jewish leaders after the exile, and some have suggested Mordecai himself. Many scholars think an unknown Jewish author wrote it some decades or more after the events, in the later Persian period or a little after. Whoever it was knew the Persian royal court well and wrote as a skilled storyteller.
audience: The first readers were Jews scattered across the Persian Empire, far from Jerusalem. They were a small minority living under foreign rulers, often exposed to suspicion and danger. The book also gave them the background to the yearly feast of Purim, which they kept together as a community.
era: The story takes place in Susa, one of the Persian Empire's royal capitals, during the reign of Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes I (around 486–465 BC). Persia then ruled a vast territory stretching from India to Ethiopia. Decades earlier King Cyrus had allowed exiled Jews to return home, but many had stayed where they were, building lives in Persian cities.

notes.1:1: The great banquet falls in the king's third year, around 483 BC, a few years before Xerxes launched his invasion of Greece in 480 BC.
notes.2:12: Esther is brought to the king in his seventh year, around 479 BC, shortly after his costly and failed campaign against Greece.
notes.3:7: This is the king's twelfth year, around 474 BC. 'Pur' is an old Babylonian word for a lot, a small object cast to choose a day.
notes.9:20: This section records how the feast of Purim began. Jews still celebrate it each year in the month of Adar, around February or March.

flags.problem: The note is attached to the wrong verse. Esther being taken to the king in his seventh year is described a few verses later, at 2:16. Verse 2:12 is about the twelve months of beauty treatment each young woman went through first, so a reader of 2:12 would see a note about an event their verse does not mention.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 2:16. Alternatively, keep a note at 2:12 that describes the year-long preparation, and put the seventh-year dating at 2:16.

flags.problem: 'From India to Ethiopia' will make most readers picture modern Ethiopia. The ancient region meant here (Cush) lay south of Egypt, roughly in today's Sudan.
flags.suggestion: Write 'from India to Cush, the land south of Egypt (sometimes translated Ethiopia)', or simply 'from India to the lands south of Egypt'.

flags.problem: The era section and the dated notes present the story as straightforward history, and the author section speaks of writing 'after the events'. Whether the events happened as told is a real scholarly disagreement. For example, Greek sources name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, and no record outside the Bible mentions Esther or Mordecai. The prompt asks for disputed matters to be noted fairly.
flags.suggestion: Add one short, even-handed clause, for example: 'Many readers take the story as history; some scholars see it as a historical tale set in a real court, since no Persian records mention Esther or Mordecai.'
